series: YouGov — Sky News Pulse / News24 Pulse (federal)
scope: Rotating one-off questions across all 22 waves (2026-01-27 … 2026-10-20 articles, plus the companion stories News24 runs beside each wave's main article, which carry some of its questions; the 2025-12-02 and 2025-12-23 waves' articles were overwritten in place by the 27 Jan story and cannot be audited). sources: Every wave's article HTML (and, from 20 Oct 2026, its companion stories) re-fetched past the News24 cookie wall plus every Infogram embed re-downloaded (kit: .matilda/n24-questions/). Embeds read but deliberately not filed are listed under not_filed with the reason; .build/news24-oneoffs-audit.mjs pages on any other unfiled one-off from the latest wave's stories.

one_offs.question: Thinking about overall immigration to Australia, including total number of people leaving and arriving, do you think we need…

rows: Immigration levels to stay about the same

prose: Their message on immigration being too high appears to be paying dividends, with only 8 per cent of voting age Australians saying immigration should be higher and 28 per cent that it is about right, compared to 64 per cent saying our immigration are levels are too high. Forty three per cent want a big decrease in immigration.
Only 8 per cent of voters think Australia’s immigration levels need to be higher, compared to 64% who want a decrease. Tellingly, 43 per cent want a big decrease.

one_offs.question: Do you support the government's social media ban for under-16s? (tracked pre/post implementation)

prose: There was strong support however for the government’s social media ban on under 16s.

Sky News asked voters whether they supported the ban before its implementation and after, and the support has only strengthened, with strongly support at 40 per cent (up 3 per cent) and somewhat support 29 per cent (steady) combining to show 69 per cent of voters support the ban, compared to only 16 per cent who don’t support it.

one_offs.question: How well has Prime Minister Anthony Albanese responded to the Bondi terror attack?
responseOptions: As well as can be expected given the circumstances

prose: The Prime Minister had his own reality check, with only 5 per cent of voters saying he responded very well to the Bondi terror attack, compared to 28 per cent who said he has done very badly.
He can take some comfort in 38 per cent of respondents saying he did as well as can be expected given in the circumstances.

one_offs.question: Current voting intention of 2025 Liberal voters (2025 vote recall × current VI)

prose: The Liberals and Nationals were down across the board compared to 2025, with primary vote for the Liberals at 14 per cent (-6.7 per cent), LNP at 4 per cent (-3.1 per cent) and Nationals at 2 per cent (-1.8 per cent).

It’s no surprise where One Nation would pick up seats, with the party outpolling the combined Liberals and Nationals in outer metropolitan seats 27 per cent to 20 per cent, and in rural seats 35 per cent to 21 per cent.

one_offs.question: What do you expect energy prices to do over the next 12 months?

prose: Thirty-nine per cent expect them to “increase a lot” and a further 38 per cent expect them to “increase somewhat”.
The data showed 63 per cent of the public believed joblessness would increase further, while one in five believed unemployment would “increase a lot”.
Just six per cent expected the cost of energy to decrease.
“Working class” respondents held the bleakest views, with 45 per cent expecting fuel to increase “a lot”.

one_offs.question: One Nation are proposing making access to superannuation before retirement easier arguing people can do what they want with their money. This has been opposed on the grounds that it will destroy retirement incomes and people already have access to superannuation in case of hardship. Do you support or oppose One Nations proposed change to superannuation?

headers: No, I am neither a parent or guardian

prose: The latest News24.com.au Pulse / YouGov poll found just 33 per cent of voters supported making it easier to access superannuation before retirement.
By contrast, 47 per cent of people said they opposed the change, while a further 20 per cent said they were unsure.
Among voters currently backing One Nation, 62 per cent supported greater access to super, while 15 per cent opposed it.
But only 32 per cent of Coalition voters supported the proposal, compared with 44 per cent who opposed it.
Opposition was strongest among Labor and Greens voters, with 68 per cent of Labor supporters and 81 per cent of Greens supporters against the change.
Among renters, 44 per cent supported the change and 40 per cent opposed it, making them one of the few groups where supporters outnumbered opponents.
But among mortgage holders, just 33 per cent supported the proposal while 46 per cent opposed it.

one_offs.question: Thinking about the financial situation in your household, would you say you are...

headers: No, I am neither a parent or guardian

prose: The latest News24.com.au Pulse / YouGov poll found just 39 per cent of Australians described their household financial situation as comfortable.
Meanwhile, 29 per cent said they were neither comfortable nor struggling. But almost one in three - 32 per cent - said their household was struggling financially.
That figure included 23 per cent who were "struggling somewhat" and nine per cent struggling "a lot".
The proportion struggling has climbed two points since January 28, from 30 to 32 per cent, while the number who are comfortable has remained stuck at 39 per cent.
More than half of renters - 53 per cent - said they were struggling, compared with 32 per cent of mortgage holders and just 18 per cent of outright homeowners.
Among households earning less than $50,000, 55 per cent said they were struggling, compared with 19 per cent of households earning at least $150,000.
Women were also more likely to report financial difficulty than men, with 37 per cent struggling compared with 26 per cent of men.

one_offs.question: The Government has cut the number of backpacker visas as part of its effort to bring down migration. Farmers and regional councils are warning against the move because they say there will be a worker shortage. What is closest to your view?

headers: Lives in semi or fully detached house
Lives in terrace or town house

prose: The latest News24 Pulse conducted from September 29 to October 3 found 62 per cent of Australians believed the government should not cut backpacker visas.
Only 20 per cent of voters supported the move while another 18 per cent said they did not know.
Among Labor voters, 62 per cent said backpacker visas should not be cut, compared with 18 per cent who supported the policy.
Sixty-two per cent of Coalition voters opposed while 22 per cent backed the measure.
Greens voters rejected them by an even larger 72 per cent to 13 per cent margin.
Even One Nation voters - whose party has proposed cutting migration to net negative for three years - opposed Labor’s backpacker cuts by 61 per cent to 28 per cent.
Sixty-six per cent of provincial voters and 71 per cent of rural voters said the government should not cut backpacker visas.

one_offs.question: Which is closest to your view? Radical Islamic extremism represents a growing concern for national security and social cohesion in Australia / Radical Islamic extremism is a minor or localised concern that is adequately managed by law enforcement / I am not concerned by the issue of radical Islamic extremism / I am unsure or don't know about the issue of radical Islamic extremism

headers: No, I am neither a parent or guardian

prose: The latest News24.com.au Pulse / YouGov poll, conducted October 13-20, found 79 per cent of Australians held at least some concern about radical Islamic extremism.
That included 62 per cent of voters who said the issue represents a “growing concern for national security and social cohesion”.
A further 17 per cent said radical Islamic extremism was a “minor or localised concern that is adequately managed by law enforcement”.
Just nine per cent of people held no concern about the issue, while 12 per cent were unsure or did not have a view.
Among One Nation voters, 85 per cent said radical Islamic extremism was a growing concern, followed by 75 per cent of Coalition voters.
The “growing concern” figure fell to 48 per cent among Labor voters and 28 per cent among Greens voters.
